**Given:** A positive integer $k$, distinct complex nodes $z_1,\ldots,z_k$, and nonzero complex weights $w_1,\ldots,w_k$.



1.1 Fix an index $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. At $z=z_j$, each summand with index different from $j$ contains the factor $z_j-z_j=0$, so $$ Q(z_j)=w_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z_j-z_\ell). $$ This is the support-node evaluation of $Q$. [given, choose, algebra]

2.1 Every factor in the product in step 1.1 is nonzero because the nodes are distinct, and $w_j\ne0$. Thus $Q(z_j)\ne0$; an identically zero polynomial would vanish at $z_j$, so $Q$ is not identically zero. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $q\in\mathbb N$, distinct real nodes $t_0,\ldots,t_q$, and real data $f(t_0),\ldots,f(t_q)$.

[F1] [[def-distinct-node-divided-difference]]: the order-zero value is $f[t_0]=f(t_0)$ and the recursive rule is
$f[t_0,\ldots,t_q]=(f[t_1,\ldots,t_q]-f[t_0,\ldots,t_{q-1}])/(t_q-t_0)$ for $q\ge1$.

[F2] [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] and [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]]: the cardinal Lagrange sum for these nodes is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $q$ taking the assigned values.

[F3] [[def-natural-numbers]]: $0\in\mathbb N$, so the order-zero case is included.

[F4] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at $0$ and preserved by successor holds for every natural number.



1.1 For each $j$ define $L_j(t)=\prod_{k\ne j}(t-t_k)/(t_j-t_k)$. Its denominators are nonzero, and $L_j(t_k)$ equals $1$ when $k=j$ and $0$ otherwise. By [F2], $P(t)=\sum_{j=0}^q f(t_j)L_j(t)$ is the unique polynomial of degree at most $q$ taking the assigned values. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 The coefficient of $t^q$ in $P$ is the displayed sum, because the leading coefficient of $L_j$ is $1/\prod_{k\ne j}(t_j-t_k)$. The sum is unchanged by any permutation of the nodes, since the permutation only reorders its terms and their symmetric denominators. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 We prove that the recursively defined divided difference equals this leading coefficient by induction on $q$ using [F4]. Since $0\in\mathbb N$ by [F3], for $q=0$ both are $f(t_0)$. For $q\ge1$, substitute the induction formula for the two order-$(q-1)$ differences in [F1] and divide by $t_q-t_0$. For an interior index $0<j<q$, the resulting coefficient of $f(t_j)$ is $$\frac{1}{t_q-t_0} \left(\frac{1}{t_j-t_q}-\frac{1}{t_j-t_0}\right) \frac{1}{\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le q-1\\k\ne j}}(t_j-t_k)} =\frac{1}{\prod_{k\ne j}(t_j-t_k)}.$$ For $j=0$, only the second recursive term contributes and its minus sign supplies the missing factor $t_0-t_q$; for $j=q$, only the first term contributes and division supplies $t_q-t_0$. Their coefficients are also $1/\prod_{k\ne j}(t_j-t_k)$. This is exactly the coefficient in step 2.1. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra, induction] ∎

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge0$, a radius $R>0$, a convergent power series $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty c_kz^k$ for $|z|<R$, and a normalized denominator solution $q_0=1,q_1,\ldots,q_n$.

[F1] [[alg-pade-coefficient-matching]]: the moment equations make coefficients of $qf$ vanish in degrees $m+1,\ldots,m+n$, while $p_k$ equals the coefficient of $qf$ for $0\le k\le m$.

[A1] Since $q(0)=q_0=1$, continuity gives a neighborhood of $0$ on which $|q(z)|\ge1/2$, so $1/q$ is bounded there.



1.1 Multiplication of the Taylor series of $f$ by $q$ gives coefficient $\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}q_jc_{k-j}$ at degree $k$. By [F1], for each $0\le k\le m$ this coefficient is $p_k$, so the coefficients of $qf-p$ through degree $m$ vanish. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For each $m<k\le m+n$, write $k=m+\ell$ with $1\le\ell\le n$. The moment equation in [F1] says $\sum_{j=1}^nq_jc_{k-j}=-c_k$, exactly the assertion that the degree-$k$ coefficient of $qf$ is zero, because $q_0=1$. Therefore every coefficient of $qf-p$ through degree $m+n$ vanishes. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Analyticity implies $qf-p$ has a Taylor expansion whose first possibly nonzero term has degree at least $m+n+1$, so $qf-p=O(z^{m+n+1})$. By [A1], divide by the nonvanishing $q$ near zero to obtain the asserted local order for $f-p/q$. This proof uses only the solvable coefficient equations; it makes no claim about zeros of $q$ away from $0$. [given, A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $a\le b$, $q\in\mathbb N$, $f\in C^q([a,b])$, and distinct nodes $t_0,\ldots,t_q\in[a,b]$.

[F1] [[def-distinct-node-divided-difference]] and [[lem-divided-difference-lagrange-formula-and-symmetry]]: the divided difference is the leading coefficient of the degree-at-most-$q$ Lagrange interpolant through the node data.

[F2] [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]: $f\in C^q([a,b])$ means $f^{(j)}$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]$ for every $0\le j\le q$, with one-sided endpoint derivatives.

[F3] [[thm-rolle]]: a function continuous on a closed interval, differentiable on its interior, and equal at the endpoints has an interior point where its derivative is zero.

[F4] [[def-natural-numbers]]: $0\in\mathbb N$, so the order-zero case is part of the stated range.

[F5] [[thm-extreme-value-r]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R$ has a finite attained maximum and minimum.



1.1 If $q=0$, which is allowed by [F4], then $f[t_0]=f(t_0)$, so the claim is $|f(t_0)|\le\|f\|_{\infty,[a,b]}$. The norm is finite by [F5]. [given, F1, F4, F5]

2.1 Suppose $q\ge1$, and let $P$ be the Lagrange interpolant in [F1], with leading coefficient $c=f[t_0,\ldots,t_q]$. The function $g=f-P$ has a zero at each of the $q+1$ distinct ordered nodes. Order those nodes increasingly and apply [F3] on each consecutive interval to obtain $q$ distinct zeros of $g'$. Applying [F3] between consecutive zeros of $g'$ gives $q-1$ distinct zeros of $g''$; continuing, after $r$ rounds $g^{(r)}$ has $q+1-r$ distinct zeros. Because $f\in C^q$ by [F2] and $P$ is a polynomial, each derivative through order $q$ is continuous and its predecessor is differentiable, so every application satisfies [F3]. After $q$ rounds one zero $\xi$ of $g^{(q)}$ remains. Since $P$ has degree at most $q$ and leading coefficient $c$, its $q$th derivative is the constant $q!c$. Hence $f^{(q)}(\xi)=q!c$, and the claimed bound follows by taking absolute values. The derivative norm is finite by [F5]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Distinct complex nodes $z_1,\ldots,z_k$, complex data $f_j$, and nonzero complex weights $w_j$.

[F1] [[def-barycentric-rational-quotient]]: $P(z)=\sum_jw_jf_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell)$ and $Q(z)=\sum_jw_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell)$.

[F2] [[lem-barycentric-denominator-polynomial-nonzero]]: for distinct nodes and nonzero weights, $Q(z_j)=w_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z_j-z_\ell)\ne0$ at each support node, so $Q$ is not the zero polynomial.



1.1 By [F2], $Q$ is not the zero polynomial. The definition [F1] therefore forms a rational function $P/Q$ for these data. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 At $z_j$, all summands of $P$ and $Q$ except the $j$th vanish. Thus $P(z_j)=w_jf_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z_j-z_\ell)=f_jQ(z_j)$, and [F2] gives $Q(z_j)\ne0$. Hence $r(z_j)=f_j$. Canceling a common polynomial factor cannot introduce a zero into the reduced denominator at $z_j$, since the original $Q(z_j)$ is nonzero. This proves the support convention. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $n\ge1$, $0\le d<n$, ordered real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, a distinct query point $x$ in their interval, $f\in C^{d+1}$, and $\operatorname{Var}(f^{(d+1)})=V<\infty$.

[F1] [[lem-hermite-genocchi-simplex-integral]]: an order-$(d+1)$ divided difference is the integral of $f^{(d+1)}$ over the standard simplex, whose volume is $1/(d+1)!$.

[F2] [[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]]: $V$ is the supremum, over finite partitions of the interval, of the sums of absolute successive increments of $g$.

[F3] [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]: $C^{d+1}$ means that the derivatives through order $d+1$ exist and are continuous on the closed interval.

[F4] [[def-natural-numbers]]: $\mathbb N$ contains $0$ and is closed under successor, so $d+1\in\mathbb N$.



1.1 By [F4], $d+1\in\mathbb N$, so apply [F1] to each $G_i$, using the same simplex coordinates for each window and using the final coordinate for the fixed point $x$. Thus $$G_i=\int_{\Delta_{d+1}}g(y_i(u))\,du,\qquad y_i(u)=u_xx+\sum_{k=0}^{d}u_kx_{i+k},$$ where all coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one. By [F3], $g$ is continuous on the closed interval. Therefore every $y_i(u)$ lies in $[x_0,x_n]$. [given, F1, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 For each fixed $u$, the sequence $y_0(u),y_1(u),\ldots,y_{n-d}(u)$ is nondecreasing: each summand $x_{i+k}$ is nondecreasing in $i$ and has coefficient $u_k\ge0$. Remove repeated values from this finite sequence and insert the interval endpoints; the definition [F2] then gives $$\sum_{i=0}^{n-d-1}|g(y_{i+1}(u))-g(y_i(u))|\le V.$$ Using [F1], the triangle inequality for integrals, and this pointwise bound, $$\sum_i|G_{i+1}-G_i| \le\int_{\Delta_{d+1}}\sum_i|g(y_{i+1}(u))-g(y_i(u))|\,du \le V\,\operatorname{vol}(\Delta_{d+1}) =\frac{V}{(d+1)!}.$$ This is the claimed total variation bound. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Distinct real nodes and data as in the Floater–Hormann definition, an integer $0\le d<n$, and a window index $0\le i\le n-d$.

[F1] [[def-floater-hormann-window-polynomial]]: $p_i$ is the sum of the local Lagrange terms $f_k\prod_{j\ne k}(t-x_j)/(x_k-x_j)$.

[F2] [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] and [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]]: the displayed local Lagrange sum is the unique polynomial of degree at most $d$ taking the data on the $d+1$ window nodes.

[F3] [[def-natural-numbers]]: every nonnegative integer $d$ belongs to $\mathbb N$.



1.1 Each summand in [F1] is a polynomial of degree at most $d$, so $p_i$ has degree at most $d$. At a local node $x_\ell$, every summand with $k\ne\ell$ contains the zero factor $x_\ell-x_\ell$, while the $k=\ell$ product equals one. Therefore $p_i(x_\ell)=f_\ell$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $d\in\mathbb N$, so [F2] applies and $p_i$ is the unique polynomial of degree at most $d$ with these window values. The constant polynomial $1$ has the value $1$ at each local node; uniqueness makes its Lagrange interpolant equal to $1$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A successful exact-SVD iteration of
[[alg-aaa-finite-sample-rational-approximation]], with Loewner matrix $L$ and
its selected right singular vector.

[F1] [[alg-aaa-finite-sample-rational-approximation]]: the algorithm selects a unit vector in the smallest right singular subspace of $L$, then forms the barycentric quotient if all weights are nonzero and returns it only after checking its reduced denominator at remaining samples.

[F2] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]: a finite-dimensional linear map has orthonormal left and right singular-vector bases and nonnegative singular values, with zero singular values in its kernel directions.

[F3] [[prop-barycentric-rational-quotient-well-defined]]: nonzero support weights give a well-defined barycentric quotient whose value at each support node is its assigned datum.



1.1 Let $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ be a full orthonormal right singular-vector basis for $L$, with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_m\ge0$ and $\sigma_m=\sigma_{\min}(L)$. For any unit vector $v=\sum_jc_jv_j$, orthonormality gives $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, and the SVD gives $$\|Lv\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sigma_j^2|c_j|^2 \ge\sigma_m^2.$$ The selected $w$ lies in the right singular subspace for $\sigma_m$, so equality holds. Hence $\|Lw\|_2=\sigma_{\min}(L)$ and no unit vector gives a smaller Loewner residual. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The right singular subspace $E$ is nonzero. If every projection $P_Ee_j$ of a coordinate basis vector vanished, then every vector of $E$ would be orthogonal to every coordinate basis vector and hence would be zero, a contradiction. Thus the least index with nonzero projection exists; the normalization and phase convention in [F1] choose a unique unit vector in $E$, also when the smallest singular value is repeated or zero. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 On the successful-weight branch, every support weight is nonzero. By [F3], the barycentric quotient is defined and its value at each selected support node is the corresponding datum. The candidate is returned only after the algorithm's reduced-denominator pole check succeeds at all remaining sample points, so its finite residual there is defined. [given, F1, F3]

2.1 Each iteration removes one previously remaining point and the budget satisfies $B\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor$. Every branch either returns immediately or proceeds to the next integer $m\le B$, so the algorithm makes at most $B$ iterations and terminates. The minimized quantity in step 1.1 is $\|Lw\|_2$; the procedure separately records $\eta_m$ and makes no minimax or uniform-error claim. [given, F1, step 1.1] ∎

**Given:** $n\ge1$, ordered distinct real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, real data $f_j$, $0\le d<n$, and $m=n-d$.

[F1] [[def-floater-hormann-interpolant]]: the support weights are
$w_j=(-1)^{j-d}\sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)}
\prod_{i\le k\le i+d,\ k\ne j}|x_j-x_k|^{-1}$.

[F2] [[def-floater-hormann-window-polynomial]] and [[lem-floater-hormann-window-polynomial-interpolates]]: each window polynomial is its displayed Lagrange sum, has degree at most $d$, interpolates the window data, and the same Lagrange basis sums to $1$ for constant data.

[F3] [[def-barycentric-rational-quotient]]: the support quotient uses weights $w_j$ in both its numerator and denominator and takes the data values at its support nodes.



1.1 Put $P_0(x)=\prod_{j=0}^n(x-x_j)$ and $m=n-d$. Counting the $m$ factors to the right of a window gives $$\mu_i(x)=(-1)^mP_0(x)\lambda_i(x).$$ Indeed, after cancellation each right factor $x_k-x$ contributes one minus sign when rewritten as $x-x_k$, and the remaining denominator factors are exactly the window nodes. Thus the cleared products agree as polynomials, including at nodes; summing gives the stated cleared-denominator identity. Away from nodes it also shows that the blend quotient with $\lambda_i$ equals the quotient with $\mu_i$ and $s$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Expand each $p_i$ using [F2], and interchange the two finite sums. The coefficient of $f_j/(x-x_j)$ in $\sum_i\lambda_i p_i$ is $$\widetilde w_j= \sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)} (-1)^i\prod_{\substack{i\le k\le i+d\\k\ne j}} \frac1{x_j-x_k}.$$ Within a window exactly $i+d-j$ factors $x_j-x_k$ are negative, so each summand has sign $(-1)^{2i+d-j}=(-1)^{j-d}$ and absolute value $\prod_{k\ne j}|x_j-x_k|^{-1}$. Thus $\widetilde w_j=w_j$ as in [F1]. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same expansion for constant data $f_k=1$ has each window polynomial equal to $1$ by [F2]. Therefore the coefficient of $1/(x-x_j)$ in $\sum_i\lambda_i$ is also $\widetilde w_j=w_j$. Dividing the expanded numerator by the expanded denominator proves that the blend equals the barycentric quotient in [F3] away from support nodes. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 At a node $x_\alpha$, $\mu_i(x_\alpha)$ is zero unless $\max(0,\alpha-d)\le i\le\min(\alpha,m)$; for these indices all its factors are positive. This index set is nonempty, and every corresponding window contains $x_\alpha$. By [F2], $p_i(x_\alpha)=f_\alpha$, so the blend has numerator $f_\alpha s(x_\alpha)$ and $s(x_\alpha)>0$. Its value is therefore $f_\alpha$, agreeing with the support convention in [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Distinct real nodes $x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d},x$, real data at them, and the local window polynomial $p_i$.

[F1] [[def-floater-hormann-window-polynomial]] and [[lem-floater-hormann-window-polynomial-interpolates]]: $p_i$ has degree at most $d$ and agrees with the data on the window nodes.

[F2] [[def-distinct-node-divided-difference]] and [[lem-divided-difference-lagrange-formula-and-symmetry]]: the divided difference on $d+2$ nodes is the leading coefficient of their Lagrange interpolant.

[F3] [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] and [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]]: for $r\in\mathbb N$, the cardinal Lagrange sum on $r+1$ distinct real nodes is the unique polynomial of degree at most $r$ taking the assigned values.

[F4] [[def-natural-numbers]]: $\mathbb N$ contains $0$ and is closed under successor, so $d+1\in\mathbb N$.



1.1 By [F4], $d+1\in\mathbb N$, so [F3] supplies the degree-at-most-$(d+1)$ Lagrange interpolant $q_i$ through the $d+2$ nodes $x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d},x$. By [F2] its leading coefficient is $c=f[x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d},x]$. By [F1], $q_i-p_i$ has degree at most $d+1$, has leading coefficient $c$, and vanishes at each of the $d+1$ window nodes. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Let $R(t)=q_i(t)-p_i(t)-c\prod_{k=i}^{i+d}(t-x_k)$. The degree-$(d+1)$ leading terms cancel by step 1.1, so $R$ has degree at most $d$; it vanishes at all $d+1$ window nodes. By [F4], $d\in\mathbb N$, and [F3] says the only degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial with these zero values is $0$. Thus $R=0$. Evaluating $q_i-p_i=c\prod_{k=i}^{i+d}(t-x_k)$ at $t=x$, where $q_i(x)=f(x)$, proves the stated remainder. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Ordered distinct nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, $0\le d<n$, and a query point in one open node gap.

[F1] [[lem-floater-hormann-weight-and-blend-identity]]: $\mu_i(x)=\prod_{j<i}(x-x_j)\prod_{k>i+d}(x_k-x)$.



1.1 If $i\in I_2$, every factor in $\mu_i(x)$ is positive: left indices lie strictly below $x_\alpha<x$, and right indices lie strictly above $x<x_{\alpha+1}$. Thus all terms in a nonempty $I_2$ are positive. If $d=0$, $I_2$ is empty. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 If $I_3$ is nonempty, its first index is $\alpha+1$ and $\mu_{\alpha+1}(x)>0$. For $\alpha+1\le i<n-d$, $$\frac{\mu_{i+1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)} =\frac{x-x_i}{x_{i+d+1}-x}<0,\qquad \left|\frac{\mu_{i+1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)}\right|<1.$$ The numerator is negative and its magnitude is smaller than the positive denominator because $x_i<x_{i+d+1}$. Consecutive terms therefore alternate with strictly decreasing magnitudes. Pairing from the first positive term gives a positive sum, including when one positive term remains. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $I_1$ is nonempty, its last index is $\alpha-d$ and $\mu_{\alpha-d}(x)>0$. Read backward. For $i\le\alpha-d$ with $i>0$, $$\frac{\mu_{i-1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)} =\frac{x_{i+d}-x}{x-x_{i-1}}<0,\qquad \left|\frac{\mu_{i-1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)}\right|<1.$$ Here $x_{i+d}\le x_\alpha<x$ and $x_{i-1}<x_i\le x_{i+d}$, so the numerator is negative and its magnitude is smaller than the positive denominator. Pairing backward from the first positive term proves the $I_1$ sum is positive. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Ordered distinct real nodes, $n\ge1$, $0\le d<n$, an open node gap, and the associated Floater–Hormann denominator.

[F1] [[lem-floater-hormann-weight-and-blend-identity]]: $D_d(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i(x)$ and $\sum_i\mu_i(x)=(-1)^{n-d}\bigl(\prod_j(x-x_j)\bigr)D_d(x)$ away from nodes.

[F2] [[lem-floater-hormann-gap-partial-sums-positive]]: each nonempty block sum over $I_1,I_2,I_3$ is positive; for $d=0$, the first two terms of $I_3$ and the last two terms of $I_1$ form positive pairs.

[F3] [[def-floater-hormann-local-mesh-ratio]]: for $d=0$, $\beta$ is the maximum of the interior minima of the two adjacent-gap ratios, and is zero when $n\le2$.



1.1 Suppose $d\ge1$. The middle block $I_2$ contains at least one index: $j=\max(0,\alpha-d+1)$ satisfies $j\le\alpha$, $j+d\ge\alpha+1$, and $j\le n-d$. Thus its window contains both endpoints of the gap and $\mu_j(x)>0$. By [F2], $s(x)=s_1(x)+s_2(x)+s_3(x)\ge s_2(x)\ge\mu_j(x)$, with empty block sums interpreted as zero. From [F1], $$|D_d(x)|=\frac{s(x)}{\prod_{k=0}^{n}|x-x_k|} \ge\frac{\mu_j(x)}{\prod_{k=0}^{n}|x-x_k|} =|\lambda_j(x)| =\frac{1}{\prod_{k=j}^{j+d}|x-x_k|}.$$ This reduces the denominator estimate to one window product. [given, F1, F2, choose, algebra]

1.2 Now let $d=0$. On the first gap, $I_1=\{0\}$ and the other nonempty block sums are positive by [F2], hence $s\ge\mu_0$ and $|D_0(x)|\ge|\lambda_0(x)|=1/(x-x_0)\ge1/h$. On the last gap it gives $I_3=\{n\}$ and the other nonempty block sums are positive, hence $s\ge\mu_n$ and $|D_0(x)|\ge1/(x_n-x)\ge1/h$. These bounds imply the claimed inequality because $\beta\ge0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Put $u=\alpha-j+1$ and $v=j+d-\alpha$, so $u,v\ge1$ and $u+v=d+1$. For $j\le k\le\alpha$, $|x-x_k|\le x_{\alpha+1}-x_k\le(\alpha+1-k)h$; for $\alpha+1\le k\le j+d$, $|x-x_k|\le x_k-x_\alpha\le(k-\alpha)h$. Multiplying these $d+1$ bounds gives $$\prod_{k=j}^{j+d}|x-x_k|\le u!\,v!\,h^{d+1}\le d!\,h^{d+1}.$$ The last inequality follows from $\binom{d+1}{u}=(d+1)!/(u!v!)\ge d+1$. Substitution in step 1.1 proves the $d\ge1$ bound. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $1\le\alpha\le n-2$, both $I_1$ and $I_3$ are nonempty. The first two terms from $I_3$ and first two read backward from $I_1$ form positive pairs. With $\Delta=x_{\alpha+1}-x_\alpha$, $\delta_R=x_{\alpha+2}-x_{\alpha+1}$ and $\delta_L=x_\alpha-x_{\alpha-1}$, [F1]–[F2] yield $$|D_0(x)|\ge \max\left\{ \frac1{x_{\alpha+1}-x}-\frac1{x_{\alpha+2}-x}, \frac1{x-x_\alpha}-\frac1{x-x_{\alpha-1}} \right\}.$$ Writing $t=x_{\alpha+1}-x\le\Delta$ in the first difference gives $\delta_R/[t(t+\delta_R)]\ge 1/[h(1+\Delta/\delta_R)]$. Writing $u=x-x_\alpha\le\Delta$ in the second gives $\delta_L/[u(u+\delta_L)]\ge 1/[h(1+\Delta/\delta_L)]$. Hence $$|D_0(x)|\ge \frac{1}{h\left(1+\min\{\Delta/\delta_L,\Delta/\delta_R\}\right)} \ge\frac1{h(1+\beta)}$$ by [F3]. For $n\le2$ there is no such interior index, so steps 1.2 cover all gaps. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Ordered real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, real data, and $0\le d<n$.

[F1] [[lem-floater-hormann-weight-and-blend-identity]]: clearing the node factors in the barycentric denominator gives $(-1)^{n-d}s(x)$, where
$s(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-d}\mu_i(x)$ and
$\mu_i(x)=\prod_{j<i}(x-x_j)\prod_{k>i+d}(x_k-x)$.
